readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
The Lord says this:
Rejoice heart and soul, daughter of Zion!
Shout with gladness, daughter of Jerusalem!
See now, your king comes to you;
he is victorious, he is triumphant,
humble and riding on a donkey,
on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
He will banish chariots from Ephraim
and horses from Jerusalem;
the bow of war will be banished.
He will proclaim peace for the nations.
His empire shall stretch from sea to sea,
from the River to the ends of the earth.

exegesis.summary: Zechariah prophesies the coming of a king who arrives not on a warhorse but on a donkey, humble and meek, yet victorious. This king will disarm the instruments of war and proclaim peace to the nations, extending his reign to the ends of the earth. The Church reads this prophecy as fulfilled in Christ's messianic entry into Jerusalem and, more deeply, in his humble kingship over every human heart.

patristicQuotes.quote: Christ is not called King as one who exacts tribute, or arms His forces with the sword, or visibly crushes His enemies, but because He rules men's minds, and brings them believing, hoping, and loving into the kingdom of heaven. For He was willing to be King of Israel, to shew His compassion, not to increase His power.
Ruth the Moabitess fulfils the prophecy of Isaiah: Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb that shall rule over the earth, out of the rock of the desert to the mount of the daughter of Sion.

cccReferences.title: Jesus enters Jerusalem as humble King
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, longing for her peace

exegesis.thematicConnection: The humble King of Zechariah is the same 'meek and humble of heart' Jesus of today's Gospel. Both proclaim that God's saving power comes clothed in gentleness, not in worldly might — a truth revealed to little ones, not to the proud.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.
or
Alleluia!
I will give you glory, O God my king,
I will bless your name for ever.
I will bless you day after day
and praise your name for ever.
I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.
or
Alleluia!
The Lord is kind and full of compassion,
slow to anger, abounding in love.
How good is the Lord to all,
compassionate to all his creatures.
I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.
or
Alleluia!
All your creatures shall thank you, O Lord,
and your friends shall repeat their blessing.
They shall speak of the glory of your reign
and declare your might, O God.
I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.
or
Alleluia!
The Lord is faithful in all his words
and loving in all his deeds.
The Lord supports all who fall
and raises all who are bowed down.
I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.
or
Alleluia!
readings.refrain: I will bless your name for ever, O God my King.

exegesis.summary: Psalm 145 is a song of praise to God the King, whose reign is marked by kindness, compassion, slowness to anger, and abounding love. The Lord upholds all who fall and raises those who are bowed down. It is a fitting response to Zechariah's prophecy of a gentle king, and a prelude to the Gospel's revelation of the Father's tender mercy.

patristicQuotes.quote: The highest of all good things is to glorify God's name in our lives. Hence He adds, Hallowed be thy name. For who is there so debased, as when he sees the pure life of those who believe, does not glorify the name invoked in such a life.
Because Christ appeared in the flesh, as the redemption and light of the whole world, well do both the heaven and earth, each in their turn, chant His praises.

cccReferences.title: The Lord, merciful and gracious, slow to anger
Love, the source of all prayer and praise
How majestic is your name in all the earth

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm names the very qualities of the King foretold by Zechariah and made visible in Christ: compassion, faithfulness, and the raising up of the bowed down — precisely the rest Jesus promises the weary in the Gospel.

readings.title: Second reading
readings.text: Your interests are not in the unspiritual, but in the spiritual, since the Spirit of God has made his home in you. In fact, unless you possessed the Spirit of Christ you would not belong to him, and if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, then he who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to your own mortal bodies through his Spirit living in you.

exegesis.summary: St. Paul teaches that Christians live no longer under the tyranny of the flesh, because the Spirit of God dwells within them. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will vivify our mortal bodies. To belong to Christ is to be indwelt by his Spirit and to walk according to that Spirit, putting to death the deeds of the flesh.

patristicQuotes.quote: Mystically, his house was the body which contained his soul, which contains within it the freedom of the mind by a heavenly vision. But God disdains neither to inhabit flesh, nor to enter the roof of our body.

Then let him who is on the house-top, that is, whose mind rises above carnal deeds, and who lives spiritually, as it were in the free air, not come down to the base acts of his former conversation, nor seek again those things which he had left, the desires of the world or the flesh.

cccReferences.title: By the Spirit we die to sin and are divinized
The resurrection of the body through Christ
In the flesh, but not living according to the flesh

exegesis.thematicConnection: The gentle King who conquers by humility (Zechariah) reigns within us by his Spirit (Paul). The 'rest' Jesus offers in the Gospel is not idleness but the interior freedom of a soul indwelt by the Spirit, no longer enslaved to the flesh.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus exclaimed, ‘I bless you, Father, Lord of heaven and of earth, for hiding these things from the learned and the clever and revealing them to mere children. Yes, Father, for that is what it pleased you to do. Everything has been entrusted to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, just as no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

exegesis.summary: Jesus lifts his heart in thanksgiving to the Father, who reveals the mysteries of the Kingdom not to the worldly wise but to the little ones. He declares the unique, mutual knowledge of the Father and the Son, and freely chooses to reveal the Father to those who come to him. Then he issues one of Scripture's tenderest invitations: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest,' for he is meek and humble of heart.

patristicQuotes.quote: If then He reveals the Father, He reveals Himself also… Herein also He instructs us that He is so one with the Father, that it is not possible for any to come to the Father, but through the Son.

Both the Father and the Son Himself are revealed by the Son, inasmuch as He is the light of our mind… For the Father declares Himself by His Word, but the Word declares not only that which is intended to be declared by it, but in declaring this declares itself.
In the mutual knowledge between the Father and the Son, He teaches us that there is nothing in the Son beyond what was in the Father.

cccReferences.title: Jesus' prayer of thanksgiving to the Father
Father and Son known only in one another
Knowledge of the Father and Son given in prayer
Christ, the Father's one perfect Word

exegesis.thematicConnection: The 'meek and humble' Jesus is precisely Zechariah's humble King, whose yoke is easy because he rules by love, not force. He reveals the Father only to those who become 'little ones' — those who, no longer walking according to the flesh (Paul), have made room for the Spirit.

synthesis.title: The Meek King Who Gives Rest
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us a single portrait of Christ our King, drawn in three strokes and framed by a psalm of praise. Zechariah foretells a victor who comes not on a warhorse but on a donkey — humble, riding to disarm the world and proclaim peace to the nations. The psalm answers with adoration of this very King, whose reign is compassion, whose faithfulness raises up all who are bowed down. Then in the Gospel, the King himself speaks: 'I am meek and humble of heart. Come to me, and I will give you rest.' His conquest, as St. Bede reminds us, is not by tribute or sword but by ruling the mind through faith, hope, and love. St. Paul shows us how this reign takes hold: the Spirit of the risen Christ makes his home within us, freeing us from the burdens of the flesh and giving life even to our mortal bodies. The yoke of Christ is light precisely because he carries it in us by his Spirit. To the proud and self-sufficient, this mystery stays hidden; to the little ones — the poor, the weary, the childlike — the Father reveals everything through his Son. This Sunday, then, is an invitation to lay down our burdens and let the humble King reign in us.
